routes.description: Establish that the surviving witness tradition and comparative methods preserve the New Testament's wording to a sufficiently high, historically appropriate degree of probability for the text to be trusted, despite localized uncertainty and the loss of the autographs.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if cumulative manuscript evidence and reconstructive method justify substantial recovery under a probabilistic standard, while the remaining meaningful variants are shown to be limited enough that local uncertainty does not defeat trust in the text as a whole.

motionBridge.description: Connect substantial probabilistic recovery, rather than certainty at every disputed reading, to the level of confidence required to trust the New Testament text.

centralBridges.description: Show that numerous, early, geographically or genealogically independent manuscripts, versions, and patristic witnesses provide cumulative access to earlier textual states.
Explain how comparison across branching written witnesses can identify copying errors and reconstruct ancestral wording even when the autographs and earliest copies are unavailable.
Establish that most variants are insignificant or readily identifiable and that the smaller set of meaningful viable disputes does not prevent substantial textual recovery.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply concrete evidence of careful early transmission or agreement between early witnesses that supports stability before the principal surviving codices.
Justify probability rather than absolute certainty as the appropriate standard for historical trust and relate the available evidence to ordinary work on ancient texts.

routes.description: Establish that textual criticism may recover an ancestral form behind the surviving witnesses without providing enough evidence to identify that form confidently with the authors' original wording, making the requested level of textual trust unwarranted.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the undocumented earliest transmission period leaves a material possibility of consequential changes shared by all surviving branches, and if later abundance, reconstructive success, or broad continuity cannot close that evidentiary gap to the autograph.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved gap between the earliest reconstructable text and the authorial wording to the conclusion that confidence sufficient for the motion has not been established.

centralBridges.description: Show that the loss of the autographs and earliest generations of copies prevents direct testing of copying accuracy during the period most capable of seeding every surviving branch.
Maintain the distinction between reconstructing the initial ancestor of extant witnesses and demonstrating that this reconstructed text is identical to the autograph.
Establish that scribal variation includes intentional, substantial, or interpretively consequential changes, so recoverable broad continuity does not resolve every material uncertainty.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why the quantity of predominantly later witnesses and the low proportion of significant extant variants do not reveal changes predating the earliest surviving evidence.
Specify why the advocate of trust must provide affirmative evidence of reliable early transmission rather than treat the absence of known total discontinuity as sufficient.

sections.title: The Standard for Recovery and Textual Trust
sections.rationale: This issue defines whether the motion requires autographic certainty or a historically reasonable degree of confidence, and therefore sets the burden against which manuscript evidence and residual uncertainty must be considered.

sections.title: The Undocumented Earliest Transmission Period
sections.rationale: The central historical dispute concerns whether missing originals and early copies leave an unbridgeable evidentiary gap or whether circulation patterns, early witnesses, versions, and patristic testimony support continuity with authorial wording.

sections.title: Reconstructing Earlier Texts from Surviving Witnesses
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether comparison among branching manuscript traditions can recover predecessor readings despite accumulated errors, and whether the earliest reconstructable text can be identified with the autograph.

sections.title: The Evidentiary Value of Manuscript Abundance and Date
sections.rationale: The number, age, independence, and coverage of surviving witnesses matter to whether the manuscript tradition provides effective cross-checks, while raising the question whether relative abundance establishes original wording.

sections.title: The Scale and Proportion of Textual Variation
sections.rationale: This issue separates the raw number of variants from the subset that is meaningful and viable, determining what the surviving variation establishes about the stability and recoverability of the text.

sections.title: Consequential Variants and the Scope of Trust
sections.rationale: Disputed readings and recognized additions test whether local uncertainty materially limits textual trust, including whether interpretive or doctrinal significance bears on confidence in the New Testament as a whole.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Having more New Testament manuscripts than survive for classical works makes comparative reconstruction easier but does not establish possession of the original New Testament text.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience question explicitly addresses Ehrman, and his answer acknowledges and then qualifies Wallace's manuscript comparison.

components.text: Whether superiority to classical manuscript survival establishes possession of the New Testament's original wording.

charity.alternative: More and earlier witnesses make reconstruction substantially more reliable than for classical works.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical probability makes total discontinuity between the surviving Gospel of Mark and Mark's writing unlikely, but it cannot determine exact identity or the extent of their differences.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Ehrman's closing statement, and the first-person closing argument continues without a speaker change.

components.text: Whether a probabilistic rather than certainty standard establishes sufficient confidence in exact or substantial textual continuity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the probability standard and identifies both what probability supports and what remains unresolved.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The advocate of textual trust bears the burden of providing evidence that the first two centuries of copying and the exemplars behind the earliest manuscripts were sufficiently reliable.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: Historical trust in ancient texts properly rests on probability rather than certainty, because consistently demanding radical certainty would undermine knowledge of ancient literature generally.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to Wallace for his conclusion, and Wallace explicitly answers Ehrman's train illustration.

response.rationale: The move justifies replacing radical certainty with the probability standard used for ancient literature generally, preserving historical trust as the legitimate issue but leaving the actual probability and autographic bridge underdeveloped.
